lines: Here's the first rule of money, and honestly, of life. You can't have everything.
Picture your weekend. You've got about ten free hours. You could mow lawns for fifteen dollars an hour, fix up an old bike to sell, study for the SAT, or just hang out with your friends.
Every one of those sounds good. But ten hours is ten hours. That's scarcity: wanting more than what you have can cover.
So you make trade-offs. More of one thing means less of another.
Now here's the part most people miss. Say you spend three hours with friends. That feels free, right? It isn't. You could have mowed three lawns and made forty-five dollars.
That forty-five dollars is the opportunity cost of hanging out. It's the value of the best thing you gave up.
Notice it's only the best thing, not everything added together. You can't spend the same hour twice.

Economists draw all your options as a curve called the production possibilities frontier. Anywhere on the curve, you're using every hour. Inside it, you're wasting time. Outside it is impossible, at least for now.
And you can push that curve outward. A better tool, a new skill, more practice. Same hours, more stuff. That's growth.
One more trap. If you already sank time or money into something, that's gone. Don't let it decide what you do next. Only what's ahead of you counts.
Companies do this exact math every day, with millions of dollars instead of ten hours. Learn to see the hidden price of every choice, and you're already thinking like an analyst.
